patterns.title: Inventory moves through the chain
patterns.lede: How many days of cost of revenue each company was holding in inventory at its year end. Read down a column to compare one year across the chain; read along a row to see one company build up and work down.
patterns.method: Inventory days = year-end inventory ÷ cost of revenue × 365, both as reported. Fiscal years end in different months, so a column is a fiscal-year label, not a calendar year. Companies with no tagged inventory are left out.

sentences.text: Equipment: of 6 companies, the most inventory any held at a year end in these years, in days of cost of revenue, was at ASML (about 289 days, FY2024), KLA (about 282 days, FY2024) and Lam Research (about 196 days, FY2024).

Chips: of 16 companies, the most inventory any held at a year end in these years, in days of cost of revenue, was at Texas Instruments (about 252 days, FY2024), Microchip (about 244 days, FY2025) and Monolithic Power (about 219 days, FY2022).

Components: of 8 companies, the most inventory any held at a year end in these years, in days of cost of revenue, was at Coherent (about 212 days, FY2026), Keysight (about 202 days, FY2024) and Corning (about 114 days, FY2020).

Devices and systems: of 14 companies, the most inventory any held at a year end in these years, in days of cost of revenue, was at Arista (about 318 days, FY2023), Ciena (about 167 days, FY2022) and F5 (about 154 days, FY2026).

Software: of 3 companies, the most inventory any held at a year end in these years, in days of cost of revenue, was at Fortinet (about 143 days, FY2023), Trimble (about 94 days, FY2022) and Roper (about 37 days, FY2019).

Cloud: of 3 companies, the most inventory any held at a year end in these years, in days of cost of revenue, was at Amazon (about 45 days, FY2019), Microsoft (about 25 days, FY2018) and Alphabet (about 8 days, FY2022).
IT services: of 2 companies, the most inventory any held at a year end in these years, in days of cost of revenue, was at IBM (about 23 days, FY2021) and CDW (about 20 days, FY2021).

patterns.title: R&D against gross margin
patterns.lede: Each company in its latest fiscal year: the share of revenue spent on research and development, against the share kept after cost of revenue.
patterns.method: R&D intensity = research and development expense ÷ revenue. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue (revenue less cost of revenue where gross profit is not tagged). Companies that do not tag an R&D line are left out.

sentences.text: The largest shares of revenue going to research and development were at Datadog (45%, FY2025), Synopsys (35%, FY2025) and CrowdStrike (29%, FY2026); the smallest at Jabil (0%, FY2026), Accenture (1%, FY2026) and Supermicro (2%, FY2026).
Gross margin ran from Jabil (9%, FY2026) to Autodesk (91%, FY2026).

patterns.title: Capital spending waves
patterns.lede: What four cloud companies and four chip makers spent on property and equipment, beside what three equipment makers took in as revenue.
patterns.method: Sums of each company’s own reported figure for its own fiscal year; fiscal years end in different months. TSMC’s figure is its own US-dollar translation, tagged in its 20-F. ASML reports in euros and is not in the equipment sum. A year appears only when every company in the group has a figure for it.

sentences.text: Cloud capital spending (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta) added up to $358 billion in FY2025, against $40 billion in FY2017: 8.9 times as much.
Chip makers’ capital spending (Intel, Micron, Texas Instruments and TSMC) added up to $75.6 billion in FY2025, against $28.4 billion in FY2017: 2.7 times as much.
Equipment makers’ revenue (Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA) added up to $59 billion in FY2025, against $26 billion in FY2017: 2.3 times as much.

patterns.title: Dependence on a few customers
patterns.lede: The largest single customer each company tags in its latest annual report, as a share of revenue - or the group of customers, where a report tags only a group. Most reports do not name the customer; the label shown is the report’s own.
patterns.method: From the customer-concentration figures tagged in each report’s XBRL data (share of revenue, not of receivables). TSMC tags an amount per major customer; its share is that amount ÷ revenue. A company with no bar tags no single customer’s share of revenue.

sentences.text: ASML: the group its FY2025 report labels “Four customers” was 61% of revenue.
Skyworks: the customer its FY2026 report labels “Company A” was 61% of revenue.
Flex: the group its FY2026 report labels “Ten largest customers” was 45% of revenue.
Marvell: the customer its FY2026 report labels “Distributor A” was 37% of revenue.
Broadcom: the customer its FY2025 report labels “Major Customer One” was 32% of revenue.
Verisign: the customer its FY2025 report labels “Other Customer” was 31% of revenue.
